title: Our response to the Commission’s call for evidence on the AI Strategy for the Cultural and Creative Sectors
content:
The European Commission concluded a call for evidence on its AI Strategy for the Cultural and Creative Sectors. Last week, COMMUNIA submitted its response (full text available as a PDF), highlighting two priorities: enabling the development of public-interest AI and safeguarding the public information ecosystem on which AI systems depend.

The strategy complements the Commission’s recently concluded call for evidence on a better copyright environment for European creativity and innovation (see our response). While some of the barriers we identify require legislative reform, the strategy can establish a broader vision for promoting access to culture, knowledge and information in the age of AI.

The cultural and creative sectors can support AI development by providing access to high-quality data. Yet several barriers prevent research and cultural heritage institutions from realising this potential:

  • National cultural heritage laws can restrict the reuse of works and artefacts that are already in the Public Domain.
  • Exclusive digitisation agreements keep around two million digitised Public Domain books from being made broadly available.
  • Paywalls restrict access to publicly funded research.

title: COMMUNIA Salon: The Rodin Case
content:
On 13 October, 14:00 to 15:00 CEST, join us for a new COMMUNIA Salon exploring the French “Rodin case” and a deceptively simple question at the heart of access to cultural heritage: Should 3D scans of works in the Public Domain be freely available for reuse, including for commercial purposes?

The dispute at hand, the so-called “Rodin Case”, started in 2018, when American artist Cosmo Wenman requested access to 3D scans of several sculptures by Auguste Rodin held by the Musée Rodin. France’s Commission for Access to Administrative Documents (CADA) backed his request, but the museum refused to release the files. In 2023, the Administrative Court of Paris piled on more pressure, ordering the museum to provide access.

However, instead of putting this dispute to bed once and for all, the case then made its way to the Council of State which,  in December 2025, reversed course. Unlike previous instances, it ruled that the collections of cultural heritage institutions do not constitute administrative documents and that the Musée Rodin was therefore not required to provide access to the scans.

title: Extending the Digital Fairness Act to the knowledge economy
content:
With the Digital Fairness Act (DFA) the Commission aims to address a number of pressing issues faced by consumers and businesses in the digital environment. This includes dark patterns, addictive design, unfair personalisation and pricing practices as well as unfair digital contracts.

In the digital environment, consumers often face situations that are not designed to be in their best interest, but rather to extract their money or time. As a result, the discussions around the DFA are already shaping up to focus on a few hot topics such as dark patterns, addictive design and protection of minors. However, the DFA also presents a great opportunity to strengthen access to knowledge and culture in Europe, and to remedy some of the failings of the digital licensing market.

title: Digital Omnibus: MEPs want to save the open government data framework
content:
During the summer, the Digital Omnibus (aka Data Omnibus) saw some welcome developments in the European Parliament. Members of the European Parliament tabled amendments both to the joint LIBE/ITRE draft report and to the JURI’s draft opinion, targeting the legal provisions we are most concerned about: Articles 32k(3) and 32r(4).

The Data Omnibus is a contentious file due to the proposed changes to the EU data protection regime. More than 1800 amendments were tabled in the main Committees alone. Therefore, we were pleased to see the (less debated) proposals concerning exclusive digitisation arrangements and open licenses not being neglected. In this blogpost, we analyse the amendments related to those provisions, and assess how they address COMMUNIA’s concerns.

title: Stop destroying videogames… and libraries
content:
In June, the organisers of the European Citizens’ Initiative “Stop Destroying Videogames” presented their proposal to the European Parliament and the European Commission. Although most Members of the European Parliament and Commission representatives voiced support during the public hearing, a subsequent Commission statement raises doubt about whether it intends to tackle the root cause of the problem: problematic licensing conditions.

After a viral campaign secured an additional one million signatures in the final two months before the deadline, Stop Destroying Videogames ultimately collected almost 1.3 million validated signatures, comfortably surpassing the required threshold. A European Citizens’ Initiative allows EU citizens to call on the European Commission to propose legislation in an area where the member states have conferred powers on the EU. To qualify, an initiative must receive the support of at least one million citizens and meet minimum signature thresholds in at least seven Member States. However, European Citizens’ Initiatives are not legally binding, and the formal right to propose legislation remains with the Commission.

title: Open letter: Protect open standard licences for public sector information
content:
Today, together with more than 30 civil society organisations from across Europe, we are publishing an open letter (also available as a PDF) to Members of the European Parliament on the Digital Omnibus proposal. We call on lawmakers to protect the use of open standard licences for public sector information and to preserve one of the cornerstones of Europe’s open data framework.

Dear Members of the European Parliament,

The European Parliament has a crucial role to play in the ongoing Digital Omnibus process: protecting the use of open standard licences for public sector information.

While the Digital Omnibus seeks to simplify EU digital legislation, it also introduces a subtle but far-reaching change to Europe’s public sector information framework. The proposal allows public sector bodies to impose actor-specific licence conditions on different categories of users.

This would represent a fundamental departure from the Open Data Directive, a key accomplishment of EU policy that has been refined over the course of over twenty years.

title: New study: Copyright challenges in open-source AI development in the European Union
content:
As the European Union actively pursues digital sovereignty, a fundamental structural misalignment has emerged between its innovation objectives and its existing legal frameworks. Across Europe, academic research consortia are utilising public funding to build open-source, public-interest Large Language Models (LLMs). However, as our newest study commissioned by COMMUNIA and conducted by Centrum Cyfrowe and Open Future shows, European open source and public AI developers are finding themselves constrained by a complex web of copyright restrictions and legal uncertainties.

The report, titled Copyright challenges in open-source AI development in the European Union (available as a PDF file), provides empirical evidence on how current text and data mining (TDM) exceptions established by the Copyright in the Digital Single Market Directive (CDSMD) operate in practice. Based on eight in-depth interviews with technical leads and data experts from prominent European AI projects—including OpenEuroLLM, Pleias, PLLUM, and SOOFI—the study maps the operational bottlenecks that hinder public-interest technology

title: Draft Digital Omnibus report: a strong step on exclusive agreements, but silence on open licenses
content:
Last week, rapporteurs Aura Salla and Marina Kaljurand published their draft report on the Digital Omnibus. The report contains an important and welcome proposal to strengthen the rules on exclusive arrangements for the digitisation of cultural heritage. At the same time, it leaves untouched one of the most problematic parts of the Commission proposal: the weakening of the open licensing framework for public sector information.

Amendment 30 to Article 32k(3) tries to address a long-standing weakness in the Open Data Directive. Under the current framework, exclusive arrangements for the digitisation of cultural resources should “in general” not exceed ten years. In practice, this formulation has proven too weak and it has allowed long-term exclusive arrangements to persist, often without review or meaningful public scrutiny. As a result, an estimated 2 million Public Domain books are currently under exclusivity.

title: JURI rapporteur tries to save open government data, but gets the solution wrong
content: The European Parliament’s Committee on Legal Affairs (JURI) rapporteur Brando Benifei has published his draft opinion on the Digital Omnibus that contains some welcome attempts to preserve the core principles of Europe’s open government data framework. Whereas the Commission proposal risks dismantling the Open Data Directive’s “open by default” approach, the JURI rapporteur rightly recognises that open data remains essential. Unfortunately, this recognition is not consistently reflected in the rapporteur’s proposed amendments. While some amendments seek to reinforce open data principles, others would undermine those same principles by allowing licensing practices that are fundamentally incompatible with them.

title: Barriers to Research: Insights into the Patchwork of Research Exceptions in European Copyright Laws and Practical Perspectives from European Researchers
content:
Today, Centrum Cyfrowe is publishing Barriers to Research: Insights into the Patchwork of Research Exceptions in European Copyright Laws and Practical Perspectives from European Researchers, a report prepared in collaboration with the Future Law Lab at the Jagiellonian University (the PDF is available on Zenodo).1 The report examines whether the European copyright framework is keeping pace with the realities of contemporary research and explores how copyright rules affect researchers’ everyday work across Europe.

Research today is international, digital, data-intensive, and collaborative by default. Scientists routinely work across borders, rely on access to large collections of publications and data, use computational methods such as text and data mining (TDM), and increasingly incorporate AI tools into their research workflows. Yet the legal framework governing access to and use of copyrighted materials remains fragmented along national lines.
